title: Mexico’s showjumping team surprise winners at the Intesa Sanpaolo Nations Cup
content:
Mexico topped the podium at Rome’s CSIO Piazza di Siena, host of the Intesa Sanpaolo Nations Cup, a CSIO5* show jumping team competition.

It was a surprise outcome that could serve as a preview of things to come at the FEI World Championships in August.

Of the 10 teams that came forward today, half are behemoths of the Piazza di Siena. Host nation Italy has won this class a record 29 times, France 20, Great Britain and Germany 11 times apiece, and the reigning titleholders, the United States, have won it six times. Meanwhile, Ireland, Mexico, and Spain have won it just once each, while Brazil has never won. Sweden and Belgium have managed sophomore wins but nothing more.

What makes a Nations Cup competition so unique is its extraordinary length. While most individual showjumping classes feature either an all-in-one jumping round, with two halves of the course judged on different speed metrics, or a jump-off format, where riders jump a qualifying round to earn the right to come back for another, foreshortened round against the clock, a Nations Cup is a marathon.

Each team completes two rounds over a full-length course, and if two or more teams find themselves on the same aggregate score at the end of those rounds, they send a representative forward for a jump-off against the clock over a condensed, technically complex version of the track.

The first round of jumping in today’s Nations Cup Intesa Sanpaolo quickly established the bogey line of the course.

One would be hard-pressed to spot any variation in the terrain of the Piazza di Siena’s main arena, which is hand-laid with new turf for the week of this show. But as the first round riders battled against the 12-fence course, it became clear that there was a minute, but not inconsequential, downhill pull from fence three, through the technically complex treble combination at five, and down to fence six, after which competitors would need to set up for the wide open water fence at seven.

That barely perceptible slope was enough to open horses’ stride patterns, allowing their weight to shift from their hind legs onto their front legs — a flattening that would wreak havoc on riders’ carefully calculated projected stride patterns down the line as horses found themselves running ever closer to the fences.

But as team after team knocked rails in that section of the course, Mexico had no such issues. Each of their competitors produced a clear round, putting them in the enviable position of choosing whether or not to send their anchor, Fernando Martinez Sommer and his horse, Joep, into the ring. With three clears already, they didn’t need saving from a drop score; the only thing to be gained was experience in the ring. Fernando decided to ride following a careful discussion with chef d’equipe Mark Laskin.

He went clear. As the second round played out, sans France and Sweden, who had both suffered 16-fault first-round tallies, the tide started to shift. Though four-fault rides were the norm in round one, upon returning to the ring to jump the same course, many of those riders adapted to the variable terrain and delivered canny clears. For Mexico, meanwhile, the run of perfect clarity was over.

Their pathfinder, the 25-year-old Carlos Hank Guerreiro, once again piloted H5 Shaq Attack to a clear, belying the fact that he had just graduated from age classes with a focused, forward-thinking ride. But second-to-go Patricio Pasquel and Chakkalou PS tipped one rail, ensuring they’d need two further clears to guarantee a clean victory. Then, as third up to bat, Andres Azcarraga and his Paris Olympics mount Contendros 2 knocked a shock three rails, adding 12 penalties to their tally and forcing the team to accept — at least — four faults in round two.

Meanwhile, the German team, who had finished round one with just four faults, had rallied in this second showing: three of their four riders had jumped clear, allowing them to discard Christian Ahlmann’s single rail and stay on four penalties.

Mexico, with one rider left to go, had two pathways ahead of them: their final rider might go clear, which would keep them on four penalties, too, forcing a jump-off ride against Germany, or they might have a rail — or more — down, handing the trophy to Germany. Had Fernando Martinez Sommer’s unnecessary round with Joep been a mistake? Would the horse, now slightly more leg-weary in the heat of the afternoon, jump less cleanly? Or would that bonus round have provided Sommer with the information he’d need to produce a clear round within the 76 seconds allowed on the clock?

Happily for Mexico, it was the latter, despite a symphony of tapped rails rattling in their cups but staying resolutely in place.

Now, Germany and Mexico could each nominate a horse and rider to represent them in the fast-paced and furious jump-off round, where the 12 obstacles of rounds one and two became eight jumping efforts over seven numbered obstacles. A new track to learn; a new set of terrain anomalies to reckon with; the pressure, too, to log as quick of a clear round as possible.

Aachen Rolex Grand Prix champion winner Richard Vogel went first, riding Gangster Montdesir. He might be the fastest rider in the game at the moment, and his round demonstrated why, breaking the beam of the finish timers at 39.99 seconds. But it wasn’t a clear. As he approached the final fence, a wide set of parallel bars placed next to the entrance to the arena, his horse lost an iota of focus and the pair found themselves on the wrong distance, taking off for the fence crucial centimetres from where Vogel had planned. They stayed on their feet, but did so in a crash of poles.

Mexican jump-off representative Pasquel found himself with a choice: he could take the pressure of the clock away and aim for a safe, steady clear round, or he could use speed to his advantage, knowing the lines that rewarded calculation and positivity. If he were to have a rail, at least he would be able to hold his head high, knowing he’d ridden like a winner. He opted to go for it.

The last and only time Mexico won this class was at the 1948 London Olympics, with their gold medal, and Humberto Mariles’ individual showjumping gold, marking Mexico’s first-ever Olympic wins.

Today, 78 years later, Mexico once again topped the podium at the Piazza di Siena, while Germany took second place on a score of eight, and the British team was third with eight penalties in the second round. The home side took fourth.

“I’m not just satisfied; I’m over the moon. I usually look at my team without making comparisons, and today’s performance gives us reason to be optimistic,” said chef d’equipe Laskin.

“Right up until the final moments of the class, we focused solely on ourselves. We knew that in a competition like this, anything could happen. I must admit, though, that competing against the Germans undoubtedly spurred us on to perform even better.

“As a coach, I do trust my team a lot. I know I can count on them every day, and today they proved that they can perform well. I expect the same commitment from them for the World Championships in Aachen, where we’ll be heading with high hopes.”

In winning, the Mexican team rewarded the country’s increased interest and investment in equestrian sport. Just 13 years ago, Mexico hosted a single international equestrian competition; this year, there will be 25. Mexico will be both a dark horse for the podium at the FEI World Championships in August.

– Tilly Berendt
